edits.html:
Incidental Proteinuria in a Well Child

Protein on a routine dipstick in a well adolescent · Is the protein still there in a first-morning urine?

Source vignette Pt — 12 yo M at a well-child visit, no illness in the past year; HR 102, RR 21, BP 102/60; normal examination · Labs — urinalysis with 3+ protein · Q — the most appropriate next step in diagnosis; options spanned a repeat urinalysis timed to posture, intravenous pyelography, renal ultrasonography, a corticosteroid trial and renal biopsy
The decision point

A well child with protein on a routine dipstick most likely has transient or orthostatic proteinuria. Both are benign. The first step is to repeat the urinalysis, before any imaging, steroids or biopsy. Transient proteinuria follows fever, exercise, stress or dehydration and clears once the trigger passes. Orthostatic proteinuria appears only while the child is upright and is most common in adolescent boys. A sample at bedtime shows protein. A first-morning sample, collected after a night lying down, is normal.

Protein that is still present on a first-morning sample is persistent and needs a renal workup. Protein with blood, hypertension or edema points to glomerular disease from the start, so that child goes straight to the renal workup.

Defining criteria Normal first-morning urine — protein-to-creatinine ratio of 0.2 mg/mg or less (0.5 or less at 6 to 24 months) with a normal urinalysis · Orthostatic proteinuria — protein in urine made while upright, with a normal first-morning sample after lying down all night · Transient proteinuria — protein during fever, exercise, stress, cold or dehydration that is gone on a repeat once the trigger passes · Persistent proteinuria — first-morning ratio above 0.2 mg/mg, or protein with an abnormal urinalysis · Nephrotic range — ratio above 2 mg/mg
Protein on a routine dipstick: the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellWhy less likely here
Orthostatic proteinuriaProtein leaks only while upright; most common in adolescent boys; benignProtein in a bedtime sample, none on waking— (the leading cause here; the timed repeat confirms it)
Transient proteinuriaFever, exercise, stress, cold or dehydration; clears when the trigger passesProtein gone on any repeat once the child is wellNo recent illness or trigger; the same repeat urinalysis sorts it out
Nephrotic syndromeMinimal change disease in a young child; heavy protein with low albuminEdema, 3+ to 4+ protein, ratio above 2 mg/mg, low albuminNormal examination, no edema
GlomerulonephritisNephritic picture; PSGN (poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis), IgA nephropathy, lupusBlood and red cell casts, hypertension, rising creatinineNormal blood pressure; protein is the only urine finding
Management ladder: incidental proteinuria in a well child
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Repeat the urine on a first-morning sample, after any fever or hard exercise has passed: dipstick, microscopy and protein-to-creatinine ratio; a bedtime sample alongside shows the orthostatic patternFirst-morning ratio above 0.2 mg/mg, or blood, casts, hypertension or edema
StopNormal first-morning sample: reassure and repeat a first-morning dipstick in 1 yearProtein returns on a first-morning sample
2Persistent proteinuria: complete blood count, electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen and creatinine; add albumin, complement or renal ultrasound as the history and exam directHematuria, hypertension, low complement, falling kidney function or signs of vasculitis
3Pediatric nephrology referral; renal biopsy is considered for those features—
Scenario bank
Pearls Up to 10% of school-age children show protein on a single screen; with repeated testing, about 0.1% do · Orthostatic proteinuria affects about 2% to 5% of adolescents, more often boys; long-term follow-up shows no progressive kidney disease · A first-morning spot protein-to-creatinine ratio replaces the 24-hour collection, which is impractical in children · A dipstick can read falsely positive in very concentrated urine (specific gravity above 1.030) or alkaline urine (pH above 8) · How NBME framed it: the key was a timed procedure, repeat urinalysis at bedtime and on waking, rather than the name orthostatic proteinuria.
Pairs with Part I Nephrotic Syndrome in a Child owns proteinuria with edema, steroids without biopsy, and the atypical features that earn a biopsy. Part II Acute Nephritic Syndrome in a Child owns protein with blood, hypertension and a low C3. Part I Hematuria carries the parallel well child with isolated microscopic hematuria.
Transferable rule In a well child with protein on a routine dipstick, repeat the urine on a first-morning sample before any imaging, steroids or biopsy. Only protein that persists on waking, or protein with blood, hypertension or edema, needs a renal workup.
Sequencing trapRenal biopsy diagnoses persistent glomerular disease; it is invasive and comes only after persistence or red-flag features are shown.
True-fact-wrong-slotA corticosteroid trial treats nephrotic syndrome; this child has no edema and no diagnosis yet.
Sequencing trapRenal ultrasonography looks for obstruction, cysts or masses; it cannot show whether the protein persists and is at most a later, selective test.
True-fact-wrong-slotIntravenous pyelography images the collecting system for anatomic lesions and strictures; it cannot show whether the protein persists.
